extracted.intended_audience: general news readers and those following corporate crisis coverage/media commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating public statements by corporate leaders during disasters — focusing on tone, empathy, responsibility, timing of apologies, and reputational consequences. Uses the BP CEO Tony Hayward coverage as exemplars of what draws criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-deafness / 'tone-deaf remarks'
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that appear insensitive to the scale or human cost of a disaster and ignore public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article framing: 'Adding to his already considerable tally of tone-deaf remarks about the oil spill...' Use as a negative signal: public comments that fail to recognize suffering or damage will be labeled 'tone-deaf' and attract criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbelievably selfish and callous sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrasing that centers the speaker's inconvenience or wants in the face of widespread harm (example: 'I'd like my life back!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted criticism: Bryan McKay calls Hayward's remark 'just such an unbelievably selfish and callous sentiment to air publicly.' Avoid self-centered language when people have died or suffered — it will be perceived as callous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of compassion / empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to demonstrate empathy toward victims, affected communities, or the environment in public remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline and commentary: 'The 'c' in CEO clearly doesn't stand for "compassion".' Critics (e.g., TreeHugger, Washington Post) emphasize that leaders should show empathy; absence of it fuels negative coverage and labels like 'a--hole' or 'clueless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Centering oneself instead of victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that make the incident about the speaker rather than acknowledging victims and impacts ('it's not all about you').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eugene Robinson's comment: the 'worst oil spill in U.S. history' isn't 'all about' you. Public statements should acknowledge victims and impacts first; centering oneself erodes trust and sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual insensitivity given loss and damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks that disregard the specific harms (e.g., deaths, environmental destruction) tied to the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: 'With 11 lives lost in the rig explosion, and an entire region's future hanging in doubt...' Leaders should tailor language to the severity of loss; flippant or self-focused comments are perceived as inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and sufficiency of apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an apology is offered promptly and whether it effectively mitigates the harm caused by the original statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes Hayward 'subsequently apologized... but the damage has been done.' Apologies may not undo the reputational impact if the original remark already shaped public perception; sincerity and corrective action matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior corporate culpability affecting sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The public's willingness to sympathize depends on corporate history and perceived responsibility for the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tyler Falk: 'when your company profits from ecosystem-destroying techniques and causes the worst environmental disaster... you're just not going to get much sympathy.' Communications must account for existing grievances and culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand to prioritize remediation over personal requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that executives prioritize restoring harmed communities/environment before making personal pleas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towleroad's retort: 'How about he gets his life back as soon as we get the Gulf back...' Messaging should emphasize action and remediation (restoring the Gulf) before personal concerns, or risk backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational and career consequences of poor remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements can trigger reputational damage and even job risk for executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Wachter note: Paddy Power offering odds that Hayward will be the first BP executive to lose his job. Poorly judged remarks during crises can accelerate calls for leadership change; anticipate and manage downstream consequences.
